empirical_claim: Apostrophe usage for numeral and acronym plurals has moved on.
basis: Ancillary usage claim; no plural-apostrophe sample.

empirical_claim: The primary function of literally is intensification, including factual expressions.
basis: Separate emphasis labels; no claim to represent all English.

empirical_claim: This is standard written, edited and published English, not a colloquial appendage.
basis: Literary/dictionary evidence supports established use; Merriam-Webster marks exaggerated sense informal.

empirical_claim: Factual or potentially factual expressions are frequently intensified.
basis: Factual reading and emphatic function often coexist.

empirical_claim: Intensifying literally is neither new nor confined to conversation.
basis: Dictionary historical evidence and later primary study.

empirical_claim: TIME frequency rises from the 1940s and peaks in the 1980s.
basis: No 2011 TIME version/export or complete historical query.

empirical_claim: TIME frequency in the 2000s returns to its 1950s level.
basis: Books are a different population and show a higher 2000s rate.

empirical_claim: Intensifier share may be slightly higher in 1920s TIME than 2000s TIME.
basis: Original openly uncounted glance; no matched historical annotation sample.

empirical_claim: Ranked COCA preceding-adverb list and counts support intensifier knowledge.
basis: Every reported count retained in 2011-other-reported-numbers.csv and 2011-historical-collocates.csv; proximity cannot establish speakers' knowledge.

empirical_claim: Just is the fourth preceding-adverb collocate and often supports emphasis.
basis: Contemporary contextual sample supports emphatic just combinations; no equivalent COCA window.

empirical_claim: Up/down/out/now co-occurrence is coincidental because they are frequent words.
basis: Would require association scores against marginal frequencies.

empirical_claim: Figuratively is by far the most common wider collocate, with 304 COCA hits.
basis: No exact span, query or corpus snapshot.

empirical_claim: Figuratively appears exclusively as part of literally and figuratively.
basis: The post itself separates the words in example 9. A new reverse-order query timed out and contributes no count.

empirical_claim: Literally/figuratively pairings can themselves involve two figurative readings.
basis: Requires context-sensitive interpretation; dual category preserves overlap.

empirical_claim: Disambiguation is a secondary function of literally.
basis: Emphasis is common but overlaps with factual clarification; not mutually exclusive categories.

empirical_claim: The intensifier function cannot be paraphrased with the adjective literal.
basis: No systematic paraphrase judgement experiment.

empirical_claim: Literal and figurative categories are not always clear-cut.
basis: Uncertain and dual readings retained separately.

empirical_claim: Clear disambiguating examples are hard to find, and rarer than prescriptivists imply.
basis: No stated comparison or prescriptivist baseline; metalinguistic readings are present in new samples.

empirical_claim: Hyperbole need not involve a clear cross-domain mapping.
basis: No independent taxonomy experiment; relevant to defining figurative versus emphasis.

empirical_claim: Numerals and quantifiers often combine emphasis with clarification.
basis: Contextual readings contain many actual quantities and durations.

empirical_claim: Speakers sometimes realise an initially emphatic expression is literally applicable.
basis: A transcript alone cannot recover the speaker's prior intention.

empirical_claim: Translation and etymological explanation are common uses.
basis: Metalinguistic sample includes translation and word meanings.

empirical_claim: Technical not-figurative literally has nothing to do with popular usage.
basis: Interpretation uses appear in corpus contexts, including ordinary conversation.

empirical_claim: The author found no technical not-figurative examples in his corpus search.
basis: New observations cannot disprove what the author personally failed to retrieve.

empirical_claim: Intensification is primary, disambiguation secondary, with degrees rather than complementary classes.
basis: Meaning/function separated; corpus scope and overlap explicit.

empirical_claim: Literally is a good indicator of nearby figurative language and a worse indicator of strict fact.
basis: Clearly figurative readings are few; measuring marker precision/recall requires a separately annotated comparison corpus.

empirical_claim: Goatly's 1997 book discusses literally among metaphor markers.
basis: Attribution preserved; book not obtained in full for this check.

empirical_claim: ATT-META researchers told the author they used literally as a metaphor indicator.
basis: No original correspondence or project implementation inspected.

empirical_claim: The Literally Blog stopped in 2009 and was reportedly founded by linguistics graduates.
basis: Ancillary website history and reported credentials.

empirical_claim: Humorous literalisation pictures may themselves be more figurative than their source phrases.
basis: No defined set or image annotation.

empirical_claim: Pinker listed 18 expressions for faeces in a linked RSA talk.
basis: Ancillary attributed number; no inference in this snack relies on it.

empirical_claim: Intensifiers add emphasis even when they add no descriptive content.
basis: The new function annotation explicitly recognises emphasis.

empirical_claim: More absurd literal alternatives reduce confusion.
basis: Requires a comprehension experiment.

empirical_claim: The author found no subtle case where the ambiguity really mattered.
basis: Absence of retrieved cases does not measure misunderstanding.

empirical_claim: Prescriptivists use literally to exercise power over insecure speakers.
basis: No causal or attitudinal study conducted here.

empirical_claim: Confusion between the two functions does not produce real consequential misunderstandings.
basis: Neither corpus occurrence nor absence of documented incidents proves this.

empirical_claim: Prescriptivists rarely support confusion claims with more than a few examples.
basis: No systematic inventory of their arguments.

empirical_claim: Nonliteral literally has been acceptable in TIME for close to a century.
assessment: Historical examples supplied; exact duration unreproduced
basis: 2011 post supplies 1920s examples; later dictionary evidence independently establishes older literary use.

empirical_claim: TIME uses literally roughly 200–300 times per decade, less than once per issue.
basis: 200–300 per ten years is below weekly frequency; does not measure all language or editorial effectiveness.

empirical_claim: A selected compilation of speeches makes repeated uses salient, though otherwise nobody noticed.
basis: Ancillary anecdote; no audience-attention data.

empirical_claim: Literally is not a buzzword or symbol of its time, on TIME evidence.
basis: No operational definition; book frequency rises later, without proving social salience.

empirical_claim: Prescriptivist empirical claims are typically factually wrong.
basis: No defined population or audit of claims.

empirical_claim: Purism and radical tendencies occur in every speech community and persist.
basis: Outside the English token sample.

basis: Unmatched queries, opaque estimates and no population/relevance denominator cannot rank annoyance.

empirical_claim: Literally was absent from the top ten results for a top-10-mistakes Google search.
basis: No dated URLs, order, location or saved pages.

empirical_claim: The top noun collocates are all quantifiers.
basis: Nine nouns are listed under a top-ten heading; means needs its own contextual check.

basis: Number/duration examples recur; no original denominator or scale annotation.

empirical_claim: With plausible numbers it is most often both intensifier and disambiguator.
basis: No validated quantitative overlap measure.
